unitKey: 2Solid, liquid, gas states and changes of stateChemistry

questions.question: What is the boiling point and condensing point of water?
What physical state is steam?
options: Liquid state
Solid state
Gas state
Plasma state

questions.question: When a liquid boils and changes into a gas, what happens to the volume of the substance?
options: The volume decreases
The volume increases
The volume remains exactly the same
The volume fluctuates unpredictably

questions.question: How do the particles of a substance behave when it condenses from a gas to a liquid?
options: They move further apart
They stop moving completely
They move closer together
They expand in size

questions.question: What happens to a Bunsen burner flame when you open the air hole?
options: It changes from a hot blue flame to a cool orange flame
It changes from an orange and sooty flame to a hotter, cleaner, blue flame
It becomes extinguished immediately
It becomes a yellow, quiet flame that does not soot

questions.question: How should a lit splint be carried safely in the laboratory?
options: With the flame pointed straight up and held close to your face
With the flame angled slightly downwards and shielded by your other hand
With the flame held horizontally and waved slowly
With the flame pointed downwards without any shield

questions.question: Which state of matter possesses the least amount of energy, and which possesses the most?
options: Solid has the least energy, gas has the most energy
Liquid has the least energy, solid has the most energy
Gas has the least energy, solid has the most energy
Solid has the least energy, liquid has the most energy

questions.question: At what temperatures can a substance in its liquid state undergo evaporation?
options: Only at its exact boiling point
Only at temperatures above its boiling point
At temperatures below its boiling point
Only at temperatures below its freezing point

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the evaporation of water is correct?
options: Water can only evaporate at exactly 100°C
Water evaporates at temperatures that are lower than 100°C
Water cannot evaporate below 50°C
Water only evaporates when it is frozen

questions.question: What change of state occurs when a substance freezes?
options: It changes from a gas state to a liquid state
It changes from a solid state to a liquid state
It changes from a liquid state to a solid state
It changes from a solid state directly to a gas state

questions.question: For a pure substance, how do the melting point and the freezing point compare?
options: The melting point is always higher than the freezing point
The freezing point is always higher than the melting point
They are the same temperature
They are completely unrelated temperatures

questions.question: How are particles arranged and held in the solid state of a substance?
options: They are free to move around and have no attractive forces
Forces of attraction hold them in fixed positions
They are held together but can easily slide past one another
They are widely separated and move in random directions

questions.question: What are the approximate values for the freezing point of water, room temperature, and human body temperature?
options: Water freezes at 0°C, room temperature is about 20°C, and body temperature is about 37°C
Water freezes at 10°C, room temperature is about 25°C, and body temperature is about 98°C
Water freezes at 0°C, room temperature is about 37°C, and body temperature is about 20°C
Water freezes at -5°C, room temperature is about 15°C, and body temperature is about 30°C

questions.question: Which set of properties correctly describes a substance in its gas state?
options: It has a fixed shape, cannot flow, and can be compressed
It can flow, fills the whole of a container, and can be compressed
It can flow, fills the shape of its container, and cannot be compressed
It has a fixed shape, can flow, and cannot be compressed

questions.question: What is located in the spaces between the particles in a gas?
options: Air
Tiny dust particles
Nothing at all
Water vapor
